title: Quentin and the Cover
premise: August Sterling, a freelance interpreter who handles deniable work for intelligence brokers, is hired to voice-match an anonymous speaker for a peace delegation that collapses within days. The voiceprint he builds accidentally authenticates against a hidden server in Tbilisi, exposing 'the Cover' — a private network that trains and places interpreters as unwitting instruments of political sabotage. Branded a loose end, August goes underground with a disgraced former analyst, Nadia Rehm, to map the network from the inside. In the end, August broadcasts the Cover's own archive using the voiceprint they built from him, destroying its credibility at the cost of his old identity; he survives, but only as someone new.
about_author: Bram Thornbury spent a decade in translation and compliance work before turning to fiction, drawing on the gray zones where language becomes leverage. He writes from a small coastal town and refuses interviews conducted in any language he speaks fluently.

chapters.title: The Delegation That Was Never Meant to Land
chapters.summary: August Sterling's POV. He arrives to interpret for a fragile peace delegation, noticing the translators around him are oddly interchangeable and tightly managed. A minor misinterpretation nearly derails talks, and August realizes it was deliberate. Emotional beat: professional unease curdling into suspicion.

chapters.title: Voiceprint
chapters.summary: August's POV. Contracted to build a clean voice model of an unnamed speaker, he records sessions in a soundproofed room, uneasy about who will use the print. The delegation collapses overnight in coordinated leaks. Emotional beat: complicity — he was handed the key without being told what it opened.

chapters.title: Tbilisi Answers
chapters.summary: Nadia Rehm's POV. A dormant server in Georgia accepts the voiceprint as authentication, flagging August's name upward through the Cover's hierarchy. We see the machine-side of the story: cold logs, automated judgments. Emotional beat: dread rendered as bureaucracy.

chapters.title: Loose End
chapters.summary: August's POV. His apartment is searched with surgical politeness; his handler offers him a 'relocation contract' that reads like a coffin. He runs, grabbing only his recording kit. Emotional beat: the vertigo of becoming disposable.

chapters.title: The Analyst Who Knew Too Much Grammar
chapters.summary: August meets Nadia Rehm, fired years ago for noticing patterns in interpreter placements across three conflicts. She recognizes the Cover's fingerprints immediately. Emotional beat: two paranoid people choosing to trust each other anyway.

chapters.title: What the Cover Trains
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Nadia explains the network's method: recruit linguists, shape them subtly, place them where one shifted phrase can topple a negotiation. August audits his own memory for edits. Emotional beat: horror at discovering your own instrumentality.

chapters.title: Safehouse Syntax
chapters.summary: August's POV. Hiding in Rotterdam, the pair decodes fragments of the leaked server index. August finds his own training file — annotated, scored, approved. Emotional beat: grief for the self he thought was self-made.

chapters.title: The Man Who Speaks in Everyone
chapters.summary: Introduction of Voss, the Cover's chief 'voice architect,' whose talent is making any statement sound native to any listener. His POV chapter shows him calmly ordering August's termination. Emotional beat: chilling banality of linguistic power.

chapters.title: Interception
chapters.summary: August's POV. A rendezvous with a sympathetic delegate turns into an ambush; August escapes by exploiting an interpreter's trick — misdirecting the hit team's radio chatter. First blood on his hands. Emotional beat: survival bought with guilt.

chapters.title: Archive of Accents
chapters.summary: Nadia's POV. Inside the stolen index she maps twelve placed interpreters across active crises — each a fuse already lit. They realize stopping the Cover means discrediting every translation those people ever touched. Emotional beat: scale pressing down like weather.

chapters.title: The Price List
chapters.summary: August's POV. A broker offers August reinstatement if he surrenders Nadia and the index. He stalls, learning the Cover fears exposure more than violence. Emotional beat: temptation wearing the mask of safety.

chapters.title: Twelve Fuses
chapters.summary: Split POV. Racing to warn placed interpreters, they reach four; two believe, one reports them, one is already dead. Each contact tightens the noose. Emotional beat: futility measured in lives.

chapters.title: Voss's Classroom
chapters.summary: Voss captures August, not to kill him but to recruit him — demonstrating how August's own voiceprint can now impersonate him flawlessly. 'You were always ours,' Voss says. Emotional beat: identity under siege.

chapters.title: Escape in Three Languages
chapters.summary: August's POV. He escapes captivity by deliberately corrupting his own accent patterns, poisoning the voiceprint's accuracy mid-escape. Costly, brilliant, desperate. Emotional beat: reclaiming authorship of his own voice.

chapters.title: Burn Notice, Literally
chapters.summary: Nadia's POV. The Cover retaliates: safehouses burn, contacts vanish, Nadia is wounded getting the final archive shard out. Emotional beat: the price of survival made physical and irreversible.

chapters.title: The Counterfeit Summit
chapters.summary: August's POV. They learn the Cover plans to detonate its masterstroke — a fabricated interpretation at a landmark summit that will ignite a war. Countdown begins. Emotional beat: terror sharpened into resolve.

chapters.title: Infiltration by Ear
chapters.summary: August poses as a Cover-trained interpreter to enter the summit's language services. Every phrase he utters is a test he must fail correctly. Emotional beat: high-wire tension, performance as survival.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Climax, August's POV. During the summit session, August hijacks the interpretation feed and plays the Cover's own archive — training files, placement orders, Voss's voice — to delegates and world media simultaneously. Emotional beat: cathartic, terrifying exposure.

chapters.title: What Voss Says Last
chapters.summary: Confrontation, alternating POV. Voss, exposed, argues powerfully that the Cover prevented worse wars — and part of the room hesitates. August answers not with argument but with the recording of his own edited self. Voss is taken; the doubt remains. Emotional beat: victory shadowed by ambiguity.

chapters.title: Aftermath in Plain Language
chapters.summary: Nadia's POV. Governments scramble to audit their interpreters; some Cover assets are quietly absorbed rather than prosecuted. Justice outside the law proves partial at best. Emotional beat: bitter, clear-eyed accounting.

chapters.title: A Voice of One's Own
chapters.summary: August's POV. He retires the name August Sterling, the voiceprint burned beyond use. Recording a farewell message in his untrained, imperfect natural accent, he finally sounds like himself. Emotional beat: quiet reclamation.

chapters.title: The Next Quiet Recruit
chapters.summary: Epilogue, distant POV. Somewhere, a young linguist signs an attractive contract with a courteous, forgettable man — and the cycle hints at beginning again. August, watching from afar, decides he isn't finished. Emotional beat: vigilance over closure.
